title: Connected talk
verifiedBy: Claude Fable 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: French subject pronouns are NEVER dropped, exactly as English's are not — and the reason is the one L1-M4 gave: je mange, il mange and ils mangent are one sound, so the ending cannot carry the person and the pronoun has to. Every clause of every turn keeps its subject, including the second and third sentences where the person is already obvious.

il and elle are the GRAMMATICAL GENDER of the noun they stand for, not the sex of a person: le livre … il, la maison … elle. English's "it" has no French twin, so an English speaker with nothing to say for a thing reaches for il and uses it for everything.
aussi goes AFTER what it adds to: je veux du pain aussi. At the head of a sentence it means something else — nearer "therefore" — and reads as formal, so keep it out of first position.

et, mais, et puis and alors join two clauses exactly as their English twins do, and in the same order English would use — and the sequencer is et puis, not a bare puis at the head of a sentence. The joining is the free part of this module; keeping the pronouns is not.

A turn is two or three SHORT sentences, each complete with its own verb and its own subject — or a short add-on that stands alone: Et du pain aussi. French does not run them together with commas the way a first attempt does — the full stop is the join.
An adjective after être still agrees with the subject, however far back that subject was named: la maison … elle est grande. The pronoun carries the gender forward from the previous sentence.
très is the intensifier — c'est très bien is "it's very good" — and it is the word L1-M8's trop is not: trop is always an excess, très is only a degree.

sentences.display: Bonjour, ça va ? Ça va bien, merci, et vous ?
sentences.cue: Hello, how are you? — I'm fine, thank you, and you?
sentences.literal: Good-day, it goes ? It goes well, thank-you, and you ?

words.note: and. It joins two things exactly as its English twin does. Its final -t never links into a following vowel, which is unusual — et Anne is said with a clear break, not as e-TANNE.

sentences.trap: The turn is two sentences and looks like one exchange. Each half is complete on its own: the answer does not borrow anything from the question, and et vous ? is a third fragment that hands the exchange back.
sentences.sound: The whole turn has two shapes: the first rises at the end, the second falls, and et vous ? rises again. That rise and fall is what makes it a conversation rather than a list.

variations.display: Bonjour, comment ça va ? Ça va bien, merci.
variations.cue: Hello, how are you? — I'm fine, thank you.
variations.changed: the fuller question, and the exchange stops after the answer

variations.display: Ça va ? Ça va bien, et vous ?
variations.cue: How are you? — I'm fine, and you?
variations.changed: the greeting dropped from the front — the turn is shorter, not different

variations.display: Bonjour, ça va ? Je suis fatigué.
variations.cue: Hello, how are you? — I'm tired.
variations.changed: an honest answer instead of the automatic one, with the speaker back in the sentence

mistake.display: Bonjour, ça va ? Ça va bien, merci, et tu ?
mistake.why: This course speaks vous throughout, and the handing-back phrase follows it: et vous ? tu belongs to a closeness the exchange has not established.

sentences.usage: The first ten seconds of almost any exchange.
sentences.mnemonic: Ask, answer, hand it back. Three moves, and et vous ? is the third.

sentences.display: Vous allez travailler demain ? Oui, mais pas ce soir.
sentences.cue: Are you going to work tomorrow? — Yes, but not this evening.
sentences.literal: You go work tomorrow ? Yes, but not this evening.

words.note: but. It joins two clauses and sets them against each other, exactly as English does, and it goes in the same place English would put it. Its final -s is silent.

sentences.trap: The answer keeps only the words that matter: oui, mais pas ce soir. English does the same — "yes, but not tonight" — and this is the one place pas stands without ne: there is no verb for ne to sit in front of. The moment a verb comes back, so does the whole pair: mais je ne vais pas travailler ce soir.
sentences.sound: meh pa suh SWAR. mais is one syllable, rhyming with lait and with the -ais of anglais, and the whole answer runs downhill from oui to the end.

variations.display: Vous allez travailler demain ? Non, je vais rester à la maison.
variations.cue: Are you going to work tomorrow? — No, I'm going to stay at home.
variations.changed: a flat refusal instead of the qualified yes; no mais is needed

variations.display: Je vais travailler demain, mais pas ce soir.
variations.cue: I'm going to work tomorrow, but not this evening.
variations.changed: one sentence instead of a turn — the same mais pas, with the plan spelled out in front of it

variations.display: Vous allez rester ici ? Oui, mais je vais partir demain.
variations.cue: Are you going to stay here? — Yes, but I'm going to leave tomorrow.
variations.changed: a full clause behind mais — with a verb back in it, the pronoun comes back too

mistake.display: Vous allez travailler demain ? Oui, mais ne pas ce soir.
mistake.why: With no verb in the fragment, pas stands alone: mais pas ce soir. ne exists only to sit in front of a verb.

sentences.usage: A qualified answer — the commonest shape in real conversation.
sentences.mnemonic: mais joins. pas alone is enough when there is no verb for ne.

sentences.display: Je veux du café. Et du pain aussi.
sentences.cue: I want coffee. And bread too.
sentences.literal: I want of-the coffee. And of-the bread also.

words.note: too, also — and it goes after what it adds to, at the end of the clause: je veux du pain aussi. At the head of a sentence it means something nearer "therefore" and reads as formal — a different job.

sentences.trap: English can put "also" almost anywhere — "I also want bread", "I want bread also". French is far less free: at the end it means "too", and at the front it does not. And the add-on needs no second je veux — Et du pain aussi is the whole of it.
sentences.sound: oh-SEE. Both syllables are clean, and the double s is a plain s sound, never a z.

variations.display: Je veux du café. Et du thé aussi.
variations.cue: I want coffee. And tea too.
variations.changed: swap the second thing; aussi does not move

variations.display: Je veux du café et du pain.
variations.cue: I want coffee and bread.
variations.changed: one sentence joined with et instead of two joined by aussi

variations.display: J'ai faim. Et j'ai soif aussi.
variations.cue: I'm hungry. And I'm thirsty too.
variations.changed: the same shape over L1-M9's avoir states — a verb back in the add-on, and aussi still last

mistake.display: Je veux du café. Aussi du pain.
mistake.why: At the head of a sentence aussi is not "too": it reads as "therefore", and formally at that. The everyday word goes at the end — Et du pain aussi.

sentences.usage: Adding to what you have just said.
sentences.mnemonic: aussi at the end adds; aussi at the front concludes.

sentences.display: Le livre est sur la table. Il est trop cher.
sentences.cue: The book is on the table. It's too expensive.
sentences.literal: The book is on the table. He is too expensive.

words.note: he — and also "it", for anything masculine. French has no neutral pronoun, so a book, a coffee and a market are all il; the noun's gender decides. Not the il inside il y a, which stands for nothing.

sentences.trap: English's "it" carries no gender and lets a speaker point at a thing without deciding anything. French makes the decision compulsory, and it is decided by the noun you used a sentence ago — not by what the thing is.
sentences.sound: eel, one syllable, with the l clearly sounded. In front of a vowel it runs straight on: il est is said ee-LEH, as one word.

variations.display: Le café est sur la table. Il est très bon.
variations.cue: The coffee is on the table. It's very good.
variations.changed: another masculine noun, and très rather than trop — and bon, not bien, for something you taste

variations.display: Le livre est sur la table. Il n'est pas cher.
variations.cue: The book is on the table. It isn't expensive.
variations.changed: the second sentence negated, with ne shortened in front of est

variations.display: La table est ici. Elle est grande.
variations.cue: The table is here. It's big.
variations.changed: a feminine noun — so elle, and the adjective takes its -e

mistake.display: Le livre est sur la table. C'est trop cher.
mistake.why: c'est points at something without naming it; here the thing has just been named, so the pronoun that carries its gender is what the second sentence needs: il est trop cher.

sentences.usage: Saying two things about one object.
sentences.mnemonic: The noun chose the gender. The pronoun just carries it forward.

sentences.display: La maison est près du marché. Elle est grande.
sentences.cue: The house is near the market. It's big.
sentences.literal: The house is near of-the market. She is big.

words.note: she — and also "it", for anything feminine: a house, a car and a table are all elle. An English speaker with no neutral pronoun defaults to il for every object, and half of them are wrong.
big. Like every adjective it agrees with the subject — grand, grande — and here the -e is audible, waking the silent final -d into a clear d sound.

sentences.trap: The adjective agrees with a noun that is no longer on the page. maison was named in the first sentence and grande answers to it two clauses later, through elle — so the agreement reaches across the full stop.
sentences.sound: el, one syllable, the vowel more open than il's. grande ends on a clear d: GRAHND, where grand alone ends nasal with nothing after it.

variations.display: La maison est près du marché. Elle est très grande.
variations.cue: The house is near the market. It's very big.
variations.changed: très intensifying the adjective

variations.display: Le marché est près de la maison. Il est grand.
variations.cue: The market is near the house. It's big.
variations.changed: everything swapped to masculine — the pronoun, the adjective, and the contraction after près

variations.display: La voiture est devant la maison. Elle est grande.
variations.cue: The car is in front of the house. It's big.
variations.changed: another feminine subject; nothing in the second sentence moves

mistake.display: La maison est près du marché. Il est grand.
mistake.why: maison is feminine, so the pronoun is elle and the adjective is grande. il here is English's "it" with a French spelling.

sentences.usage: Describing a place across two sentences.
sentences.mnemonic: The gender crosses the full stop, and takes the adjective with it.

sentences.display: Je vais au marché, et puis je rentre.
sentences.cue: I'm going to the market, and then I'm going home.
sentences.literal: I go at-the market, and then I go-home.

words.note: and then — it sequences two things, and speech opens the second half with et puis, not a bare puis. The subject pronoun still follows it: et puis je rentre.
rentrer, to go home, to get back — the verb French uses where English says "go home". je rentre · je vais rentrer · je suis rentré (être, like aller). à la maison after it is optional.

sentences.trap: Going home has its own verb. English builds it from "go" and "home", and je vais à la maison is what that produces — understood, and not what a French speaker says. rentrer is the word, on its own or with à la maison behind it, and in the past it takes être: je suis rentré.
sentences.sound: ay pwee zhuh RAHNTR. puis is one syllable, shorter than it looks, with its -s silent; rentre is nasal at the front and ends on a swallowed -tre.

variations.display: Je vais au marché, et puis je vais travailler.
variations.cue: I'm going to the market, and then I'm going to work.
variations.changed: a plan rather than a place after et puis

variations.display: Je vais au marché, et puis je rentre à la maison.
variations.cue: I'm going to the market, and then I'm going back home.
variations.changed: rentrer can carry à la maison behind it — the same verb, with the place spelled out

variations.display: Ce soir je vais manger, et puis je vais dormir.
variations.cue: This evening I'm going to eat, and then I'm going to sleep.
variations.changed: the same sequencing over two plans

mistake.display: Je vais au marché, et puis rentre.
mistake.why: The pronoun stays, even behind et puis: et puis je rentre. Nothing in French lets the verb stand without its subject.

sentences.mnemonic: et puis leads the second half; aussi trails it. Neither of them replaces the pronoun.

sentences.display: J'ai faim. Alors je vais manger.
sentences.cue: I'm hungry. So I'm going to eat.
sentences.literal: I-have hunger. So I go eat.

words.note: so, in the sense of "in that case" — it opens the second sentence and draws the consequence. The conversational cousin of L1-M9's donc: donc joins two halves of one sentence, alors starts a new one.

sentences.trap: donc and alors both translate "so", and English gives no clue which to use. The difference is where they sit: donc inside a sentence after a comma, alors at the head of the next one.
sentences.sound: a-LOR, with the r in the throat and the -s silent. It is one of the most-heard words in spoken French.

variations.display: J'ai faim, donc je vais manger.
variations.cue: I'm hungry, so I'm going to eat.
variations.changed: donc inside one sentence instead of alors opening a second

variations.display: J'ai soif. Alors je vais boire de l'eau.
variations.cue: I'm thirsty. So I'm going to drink water.
variations.changed: another avoir state and another plan behind the same word

variations.display: J'ai faim. Alors je vais acheter du pain.
variations.cue: I'm hungry. So I'm going to buy bread.
variations.changed: a different consequence — the frame does not move

mistake.display: J'ai faim. Donc je vais manger.
mistake.why: donc belongs inside a sentence, after a comma; alors is what opens a new one. Neither is wrong French on its own, but this turn wants alors.

sentences.usage: Explaining what you are about to do.

sentences.display: Hier j'ai vu un film. C'est un très bon film.
sentences.cue: Yesterday I saw a film. It's a very good film.
sentences.literal: Yesterday I-have seen a film. It-is a very good film.

words.note: very — a plain degree word, and the one L1-M8's trop is not. c'est très cher is "it is very expensive", a description; c'est trop cher is "it is TOO expensive", a complaint. Its final -s is silent.
good — an adjective, and one of the few French puts before its noun: un bon prix, not un prix bon. It agrees — bon, bonne — and the -e wakes the nasal vowel into a plain one: two different sounds.

sentences.trap: The two sentences are in two different tenses and the turn is perfectly ordinary: the seeing was yesterday, the film is still good today. And the verdict is c'est, not il est: a thing is judged with c'est bien or c'est un bon film, while il est bien would say it is well placed or in good shape.
sentences.sound: say uhn treh bohn FEELM. très keeps its -s silent and its vowel open, as the grave accent shows; bon is nasal and runs straight into film.

variations.display: Hier j'ai vu un film. C'est un bon film.
variations.cue: Yesterday I saw a film. It's a good film.
variations.changed: très taken away — a plain verdict instead of a strong one

variations.display: Hier j'ai vu Anne. Elle est très contente.
variations.cue: Yesterday I saw Anne. She's very happy.
variations.changed: a person rather than a thing, so elle and a feminine adjective

variations.display: J'ai vu le film. C'est bien.
variations.cue: I saw the film. It's good.
variations.changed: no time word, no noun and no intensifier — c'est bien is the plainest verdict there is

mistake.display: Hier j'ai vu un film. C'est un très bien film.
mistake.why: bien is L1-M2's adverb and cannot describe a noun; in front of film the word is bon: un très bon film. Without the noun, praise is c'est bien.

sentences.usage: Reporting something and giving a verdict on it.

sentences.display: C'est combien ? C'est dix euros. C'est un bon prix.
sentences.cue: How much is it? — It's ten euros. — That's a good price.
sentences.literal: It-is how-much ? It-is ten euros. It-is a good price.

words.note: price — masculine, so le prix and un bon prix. Its -x is silent, and the word is spelled the same in the singular and the plural: un prix, deux prix.

sentences.trap: L1-M1 taught that adjectives follow the noun, and most of them do. bon — met on the sentence before this one — is one of the handful that go in front, and there is no way to tell from the word which set it belongs to: it is learned with the adjective.
sentences.sound: bohn, nasal, with the n never sounded; bonne is BON, with the n clear and the vowel plain. prix is pree.

variations.display: C'est combien ? C'est vingt euros. C'est trop cher.
variations.cue: How much is it? — It's twenty euros. — That's too expensive.
variations.changed: the same three-move turn ending in a complaint instead of approval

variations.display: C'est un bon livre.
variations.cue: It's a good book.
variations.changed: one sentence, with bon still in front of its noun

variations.display: C'est une bonne voiture.
variations.cue: It's a good car.
variations.changed: a feminine noun — bonne, and the n is heard

mistake.why: bon goes in front of its noun: un bon prix. Most French adjectives follow, and this is one of the few that does not.

sentences.usage: A three-move exchange at a counter.
sentences.mnemonic: Most adjectives follow. bon is one of the few that leads.

sentences.display: Je vais au marché demain. Vous voulez venir ?
sentences.cue: I'm going to the market tomorrow. Do you want to come?
sentences.literal: I go at-the market tomorrow. You want come ?

words.note: to come — the bare form, following voulez with nothing between them, as L1-M3's frame demands. It is also on L1-M5's être list, so its past would be je suis venu — a later level's business.

sentences.trap: The invitation is the second half of a turn and it keeps its vous, which is what makes it an invitation rather than an announcement. Dropping the pronoun would leave voulez venir ?, which is not a French sentence at all.
sentences.sound: vuh-NEER, with both r's in the throat. voulez venir runs as four light syllables with the stress only at the very end.

variations.display: Je vais au marché demain. Vous voulez venir avec moi ?
variations.cue: I'm going to the market tomorrow. Do you want to come with me?
variations.changed: avec and a pronoun after it — the phrase that makes the invitation explicit

variations.display: Je vais au marché demain. Vous allez venir ?
variations.cue: I'm going to the market tomorrow. Are you going to come?
variations.changed: allez instead of voulez: asking about the plan rather than the wish

variations.display: Ce soir je vais voir un film. Vous voulez venir ?
variations.cue: This evening I'm going to see a film. Do you want to come?
variations.changed: a different plan in the first half; the invitation is unchanged

mistake.display: Je vais au marché demain. Voulez venir ?
mistake.why: The subject pronoun is not optional, ever: Vous voulez venir ? A French verb cannot stand on its own the way an English imperative can.

sentences.usage: Inviting someone along — the last thing L1 teaches you to do.
sentences.mnemonic: Ten rungs, one rule that never bent: the pronoun stays.
